rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Except for close relatives, Islam requires men and women to sit separately in the home.
rows.anchor: except for close relatives, Islam requires that other men should sit separately.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Restraining the eyes matters because sight is the first connection between men and women; obeying this rule guards against many satanic temptations.
rows.anchor: The directive of restraining the eyes is a very important one because it is the eyes that form the first connection between men and women.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Decent clothing is the best means of guarding private parts.
rows.anchor: Guarding private parts can best be achieved by wearing decent clothes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Modern fashion has displaced clothing's purpose of covering the body with ugly embellishment, and men now wear indecent attire even to believers' homes.
rows.anchor: Such are the innovations of fashion these days that the real purpose of dress – hiding the body – has totally vanished.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The house precautions promote moral purity only when people remember that God knows even their most secret actions; without that awareness, they will not restrain their eyes or cover themselves.
rows.anchor: this can only be the case when a person observes these precautions while fully keeping mind that God is aware

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Women too must lower their gaze and guard their private parts before non-maḥrams, conceal adornments except what cannot be hidden, and observe the listed exceptions.
rows.anchor: These verses direct women to lower their gazes as well if a non-maḥram person enters the house, to guard their private parts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Women should not walk in a way that attracts attention to the adornments they wear.
rows.anchor: not in manner that attracts attention to the adornments they may be wearing.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zīnat includes both clothing and jewelry; since outer clothing and some hand jewelry cannot easily be concealed, the exception relieves women of extraordinary efforts and requires hiding only what can be concealed without much bother.
rows.anchor: Adornments ( zīnat) include dress as well as jewellery. Neither can each of these things be totally concealed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khimār means a shawl or covering.
rows.anchor: The Arabic word khimār means a shawl or covering.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A covering is essential in women's dress, and before non-maḥrams women must cover their chests and necklines as well as their heads and backs.
rows.anchor: it is essential that women hide their chests and necklines besides their heads and backs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The category of fathers includes paternal uncles, fathers, and grandfathers; the verse lists prominent maḥrams but encompasses all relatives covered by the rule.
rows.anchor: includes paternal uncles, father and grandfather. Only the most prominent of maḥram relatives are enumerated

rows.speaker: Some jurists
rows.claim: Some jurists limit “their women” to Muslim women, a restriction Islahi rejects.
rows.anchor: Some jurists say that only Muslim women are included

rows.speaker: al-Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī reads this as women of acquaintance and service, which Islahi considers more correct than the Muslim-women-only view.
rows.anchor: Zamakhsharī in this regard is more correct. He is of the opinion that this refers to women of acquaintance and service.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revealing adornments before every unfamiliar woman carries risks, since some women may use such knowledge deceptively.
rows.anchor: displaying ornaments before all types of women who are strangers is not without its hazards.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression for those possessed by the right hand includes both enslaved men and enslaved women.
rows.anchor: implies both slave-men and slave-women.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If only enslaved women were intended, the wording would have said “their slave-women”; the expression used is the common term for both sexes.
rows.anchor: Had only slave-women been implied by this expression, then the appropriate words would have been

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A separate mention of enslaved women would be redundant because the previously named category of women of acquaintance and service already includes slave women and maidservants.
rows.anchor: the category which as, has been explained, includes both women with whom one is generally acquainted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says the slave-women-only inference conflicts with explicit Quranic injunctions.
rows.anchor: this inference is also against certain explicit injunctions of the Qur’ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dependent men exempted from the restrictions are old, disabled, blind, or lame men who no longer have sexual desire.
rows.anchor: old, handicapped, blind and lame men who no longer have sexual desires.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If such men are supported by and live with a household, the earlier restrictions do not apply; Islahi includes old servants in this group.
rows.anchor: being provided for by the family of the house and they also live there, then the above mentioned restrictions do not apply to them as well.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Old servants must still seek permission at the three occasions specified in 24:58.
rows.anchor: However, they must seek permission on three occasions which is mentioned in verse 58 ahead.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The children meant are those not yet aware of sex and not attracted to women's sexual organs as adult men are.
rows.anchor: children who do not have awareness about sex as yet, and they do not feel attracted to the sexual organs of a woman

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Children initially did not need permission, but a later rule requires them to seek it at three occasions.
rows.anchor: Initially, they were not required to take permission but later they were also asked to seek permission on three occasions.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition addresses the urge to display adornments: women moving through the house before non-maḥrams should not stamp their feet so their jewelry does not ring.
rows.anchor: she should not stamp her feet on the ground so that the ringing of jewellery is heard.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing call to repentance addresses the whole Muslim society: everyone should reform their conduct and adopt Quranic life, the path to success.
rows.anchor: everyone should try to mend their ways and adopt the life recommended by the Qur’ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi points to the conditions of success in 22:76 and 23:1.
rows.anchor: The conditions of success are stated in verse 76 of Sūrah al-Ḥajj and verse 1 of Sūrah al-Mu’munūn.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The later rule in 24:58 permits both enslaved men and women to enter without permission except at three times; the reason is that household members come and go among each other, supporting the view that both sexes are meant here.
rows.anchor: both slave-men and slave-women are permitted to enter houses without permission except on three occasions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi sides with jurists who include enslaved men and women in this category, while requiring them to observe the restrictions stated in 24:58.
rows.anchor: For this reason, I regard the view of those jurists to be correct who include both slave-men and slave-women in this directive.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The slavery discussion is now academic because slavery has been abolished; Islahi says Islam historically took the first step toward its abolition.
rows.anchor: slavery has been abolished from this world and for this the very first step was historically taken by Islam.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Today adult servants must seek permission before entry and, in the home, they and its women must observe the stated limits.
rows.anchor: As far as adult servants are concerned, in my opinion, it is essential for them to abide by all the restrictions mentioned above.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ayyām is the plural of ayyim and refers to a man or woman without a spouse, broadly including unmarried men and women.
rows.anchor: It refers to a husband who does not have a wife and also to woman who does not have a husband.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣāliḥ refers to people physically able and morally upright; Arabic uses it in this comprehensive sense.
rows.anchor: those who are able both with regard to their physical strength and moral conduct.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unmarried people leave society exposed to sexual wrongdoing, Satan's temptation, illicit relations, and slander; poverty and restrictive family, tribal, and especially anti-widow customs contribute, so society should enable suitable marriages and help the poor.
rows.anchor: A wide fissure left in the society for moral evils and Satan’s luring to infiltrate into is the existence of men and women who are not married.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Society should marry able-bodied and morally sound enslaved men and women; their ability means handling responsibilities and understanding rights and duties, and marriage raises their social status as they gradually join the free.
rows.anchor: This directive has been given to raise the moral and social status of slaves and gradually they become part of free men and women.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The instructions for men and women in the preceding verses concern dress inside the home; what women should wear outside is addressed in Sūrah al-Aḥzāb, and Islahi says his booklet Qur’ān and Pardah explains both Quranic directives.
rows.anchor: is given in Sūrah al-Aḥzāb and not here.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi criticizes readers who fail to find these explicit Quranic dress instructions, accusing them of turning their restraint away from the Qur’an instead of from the opposite sex.
rows.anchor: After these explicit directives, those who are not able to find such directives

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poverty should not prevent marriage: it does not increase poverty, and God favors and assists those who marry to protect their faith and character.
rows.anchor: those who are poor and others too should rest assured that marriage does not increase poverty. It increases God’s grace and sustenance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Marriage develops the capacities of both spouses: unmarried men have dormant abilities and unmarried women lack support, while their joint effort after marriage can bring improvement in circumstances through God's blessing.
rows.anchor: when both of them start to strive in life together, the Almighty blesses them in their struggle and their circumstances also change for the better.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of God as capacious and knowing reinforces the promise because He knows everyone's needs and circumstances.
rows.anchor: God is fully aware of the needs and circumstances of everyone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The society-wide marriage directive does not release individuals from moral responsibility: they should remain chaste and wait for God's grace, trusting that He will open avenues for those protecting faith and character.
rows.anchor: The previous directive was meant for the society. However, this does not absolve an individual of his moral responsibilities.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kitāba is a contract in which a slave secures emancipation by paying a specified amount over a set period or performing an agreed task, after which the master must free him.
rows.anchor: It means that a slave seeks his emancipation from his master by paying him a certain amount in a specific period of time

rows.speaker: Scholars
rows.claim: Scholars generally regard the instruction to grant mukātabah as recommendatory.
rows.anchor: Scholars generally regard this directive to be recommendatory.

rows.speaker: ʿUmar (rta), Ibn Sīrīn and Dā’ūd
rows.claim: ʿUmar, Ibn Sīrīn, and Dā’ūd hold that a master is obligated to make a requesting slave a mukātab; Islahi agrees with their view.
rows.anchor: ‘Umar (rta), Ibn Sīrīn and Dā’ūd regard it to be imperative.
